A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SCP/LUR research work. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial reorganization and additions.

before.justification: V1 reports original Gaussian-process experiments, forecasting results for five models in Table 1, and channel-level, temporal, frequency-band, and predictability-stratified analyses.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds parameter sensitivity studies, variable-history experiments, multivariate synthetic results, and Traffic/ILI evaluations.

M1.justification: The original scalar SCP/LUR formulas remain, but Appendix B adds multivariate SCP and LUR algorithms using matrix-valued spectra, nonlinear SCP through feature mappings, and a boundary-pairing procedure for unequal history/future lengths. V1 listed multivariate extension only as future work. The nonlinear variant is formulated without corresponding empirical evaluation.

E1.justification: V2 retains the six original forecasting datasets and Gaussian-process toy study, and adds Traffic and ILI, extending coverage to transportation and epidemiology. Appendix C.2 also introduces a distinct multivariate sinusoid-mixture task with progressively revealed informative input channels.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains the same five reported models: iTransformer, TimeMixer, DLinear, PatchTST, and TimesNet. The new benchmarks use this same set. Within the predictability-drift comparison in Figure 3, however, v2 adds PatchTST alongside DLinear, whereas v1 displayed only DLinear.

E3.justification: The original Table 1 protocol remains unchanged. V2 adds controlled Welch-parameter sweeps, varying history lengths at fixed forecast horizon 336, a 20-versus-30-band comparison, and frequency-centroid summaries. Its multivariate synthetic study specifies 640 independent sequences. Figure 3's stated horizon changes from 96 to 336; this establishes a reported setting change, not that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's calibration and diagnostic case studies, v2 tests sensitivity to Welch settings (Section 5.6), history length (Section 5.7), and frequency partitioning (Appendix C.1). Appendix C.2 tests whether multivariate predictability increases when additional informative channels become observable. These directly examine estimator stability and information sensitivity.

E5.justification: Figure 6 adds LUR error bars, including to the retained 30-band analysis, although their statistical basis is unspecified. Table 5 and Figure 7 explicitly report standard deviations across 640 independent synthetic sequences. The original toy study still averages three trials; no increase in repeated model-training runs or seeds is established.

E6.justification: Table 1's numerical results are unchanged. V2 adds sensitivity, centroid, multivariate, and Traffic/ILI results. In Table 5, mean multivariate predictability rises from 0.117 to 0.848 as observed inputs increase from one to six. Table 6 reports iTransformer's lowest MSE across Traffic horizons, PatchTST's best ILI MSE at horizon 60 (1.758), and TimeMixer's at 72 (1.928). These are newly reported results, not same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: Appendix B introduces matrix-valued Wiener projection and residual derivations, formal multivariate and feature-dependent nonlinear predictability definitions, unequal-window spectral construction, and mathematical formulations for proposed downstream uses. It also adds a sine/cosine counterexample demonstrating zero-lag correlation's failure to detect phase-shifted linear dependence. These formulations and derivations are absent from v1.

C1.justification: SCP/LUR diagnostics, predictability drift, and complementary architectural strengths remain the headline contributions. V2 refines the framing from separating intrinsic irreducible unpredictability toward an empirically calibrated linear instance-difficulty reference, drops the 'first' priority claims, and replaces the abstract's categorical complex-versus-linear trade-off with broader architectural complementarity.

C2.justification: V2 adds an interpretation of nonlinear/nonstationary components as effective noise under finite sampling and discusses feature-dependent nonlinear predictability and additional applications. It weakens v1's assertion that predictability fluctuations 'always dominate' errors to partial confounding and presents architectural frequency selectivity as a plausible explanation. V1's explicit within-window stationarity limitation is no longer stated as such, although the Gaussian/stationary theoretical interpretation remains.

D1.justification: The original toy, backbone, and Welch implementation details are retained in Appendix A, formerly Appendix C. V2 adds dataset split counts in Table 4 and a detailed multivariate synthetic-data recipe. It removes v1's statement that code, configurations, and scripts were released; the PDFs do not establish any actual change in resource availability.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion largely remains. V2 adds coherence references by Mandel and Wolf (1976) and Wang et al. (2019), while removing Ehrenberg and Bound (1993), Li et al. (2019), and Zhou et al. (2021). Appendix B.5 adds positioning against time-domain correlation diagnostics, and the main text drops priority claims.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method explanations, experimental narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Experimental setup moves from Appendix C to A, with new appendices for extensions and supplementary experiments. Future applications are redistributed into the Impact Statement and Appendix B.4, while the standalone LLM-use and limitations sections disappear.

P2.justification: V2 reformats the main text into two columns and restacks several multipanel figures. Figure 3 is redrawn, Figure 4 gains centroid labels, and Figure 5 uses distinct model markers while retaining its plotted results. Tables 2–6 and Figures 6–7 add displays; Figure 6b redisplays the existing 30-band curves with error bars.

improvement.justification: The targeted robustness studies in Sections 5.6–5.7 and Appendix C, broader benchmark validation, and more careful linear-reference framing strengthen support for the retained diagnostic framework. The net gain is limited by inconsistencies in the new optional extensions: Eq. 15's equality does not hold with the stated positive regularization, and Eq. 33's negative exponent favors low-predictability instances despite claiming the opposite.
